title: Raman Optical Activity Induced by Ferroaxial Order in NiTiO3
claims: A large Raman optical activity (cross-circular LR/RL intensity difference, g_ROA up to about 1 for the E_g(1) mode at 785 nm) appears in the centrosymmetric, non-magnetic ferroaxial crystal NiTiO3.
The sign of g_ROA reverses between the front and back faces of a single-domain crystal, so the signal follows the orientation of the ferroaxial vector.
The same sign of g_ROA in Stokes and anti-Stokes spectra shows that the ROA is non-magnetic in origin.
The ROA is selectively enhanced at 785 nm by resonance with the Ni2+ d-d transition, being weak at 532 nm and absent at 633 nm.
Symmetry analysis and tight-binding calculations show that the ROA originates directly from the ferroaxial order and persists within the electric dipole approximation.
Spatial maps of g_ROA correlate with the ferroaxial domain structure, so Raman spectroscopy can image ferroaxial domains.
summary: The paper reports circularly polarized Raman spectroscopy on single- and multidomain NiTiO3 crystals, finding a large difference between LR and RL intensities of E_g phonons at 785 nm that reverses sign between the two faces of a single-domain crystal and maps onto ferroaxial domains. A symmetry analysis and a tight-binding model are used to argue that ferroaxial order makes the two rotational E_g components inequivalent, producing natural ROA within the electric dipole approximation, enhanced by resonance with the Ni2+ d-d transition.
strengths: The effect is large and clear in the raw spectra and reverses sign between the front and back faces of the same crystal with nearly equal magnitude for E_g(1), which rules out a simple fixed instrumental offset.
Several internal checks fit the proposed picture: no LL/RR asymmetry for the A_g modes, the same sign in Stokes and anti-Stokes, and a strong dependence on excitation wavelength.
The high-resolution line scan across a domain wall shows a sharp sign change of g_ROA with raw LR/RL spectra on both sides, evidence that the contrast is spatially local.
The symmetry derivation of the circular-basis E_g Raman tensors and the essential-parameter analysis tying the effect to t_ax are explicit, general and easy to check.

issues.claim: Mechanism: ferroaxial order alone within electric dipole approximation
issues.headline: Absorption-induced phase is a necessary second ingredient, left out of mechanism
issues.issue: With the E_g Raman tensors allowed in -3, I_LR - I_RL is proportional to Im(c d*), so the asymmetry needs both the ferroaxial-allowed component d and a relative phase from absorption or resonance; with real, non-resonant tensors it vanishes, as the paper's own model (below the JDOS onset) and the 633 nm null show. The mechanism is therefore a ferroaxial-allowed version of the absorption-based explanation of Ref. [4], not a separate one, and the Sec. S3 arguments that interference cannot give ROA and that resonance does not change selection rules need reconciling with this.

evidence.quote: The static ferroaxial distortion provides a preferred sense of rotation in the lattice, rendering the two rotational components

issues.fix: State the Im(c d*) condition in the main text (ferroaxial order supplies d, absorption supplies the phase) and revise the abstract and conclusion so the probe is described as working under resonant or absorbing conditions. Show model curves where g_ROA goes to zero as t_ax goes to 0 and as the smearing goes to 0 away from resonance, explain what the tight-binding calculation adds beyond this condition, and state how the mechanism relates to and differs from Refs. [4-7].
issues.fix_scoped: Our symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations of phonons, and tight-binding model calculations show that the ferroaxial order allows an off-diagonal E_g Raman tensor component which, together with the phase supplied by resonant absorption, produces the cross-circular ROA within the electric dipole approximation.

issues.headline: Bulk origin not separated from near-surface or field-induced signal
issues.issue: Any surface breaks inversion, and n·A is a pseudoscalar of opposite sign on the two faces, so a surface-localized gyrotropic layer or electrogyration from a surface or depletion field would reproduce the front/back reversal and domain contrast. That would be ROA from an inversion-broken region, not from the centrosymmetric bulk stressed in the title and abstract.

evidence.quote: In this study, we report the observation of a remarkably large ROA in a three-dimensional centrosymmetric bulk crystal of NiTiO3, a material known to exhibit ferroaxial order.

issues.fix: Measure g_ROA(E_g(1)) as a function of confocal focal depth through the 60 µm crystal and compare with the depth resolution and the 785 nm absorption length; ideally also measure g_ROA under an applied electric field along c to bound any electrogyration contribution.
issues.fix_scoped: In this study, we report the observation of a remarkably large ROA in a centrosymmetric crystal of NiTiO3, a material known to exhibit ferroaxial order; whether the signal arises from the bulk or from a near-surface region within the optical probing depth remains to be established.

edit_scoped.after: In this study, we report the observation of a remarkably large ROA in a centrosymmetric crystal of NiTiO3, a material known to exhibit ferroaxial order; whether the signal arises from the bulk or from a near-surface region within the optical probing depth remains to be established.

issues.headline: Instrumental baseline and circular polarization purity are not characterised
issues.issue: A single QWP after a non-polarizing beam splitter defines both polarizations, and beam-splitter phase, QWP retardance error at each wavelength and high-NA depolarization could each give a fixed-sign LR/RL imbalance; Table S4 shows a common front/back offset of about -0.03, larger than the ±0.02 error, E_g(4) does not reverse, and the all-positive 532 nm front-only values cannot be separated from an offset. A_g(3) leaks into the 633 nm cross-circular spectrum, so the 633 nm null may be partly instrumental, and the off-sample g_ROA ≈ 0 control is only a ratio of noise.

evidence.quote: Although much weaker, we indeed observe discernible ROA signals at 532 nm, while ROA was negligibly small at 633 nm.
evidence.location: Sec. S5; Table S4; Fig. S5; Fig. S1

issues.fix: Specify the QWP and beam splitter, report the circular extinction ratio at each wavelength, measure back-face spectra at 532 and 633 nm, measure non-ferroaxial -3m references (e.g. α-Al2O3 or calcite, and an absorbing one such as ruby) and preferably a chiral reference such as α-quartz under identical conditions, and subtract the measured instrumental offset.
issues.fix_scoped: At 532 nm the front-surface values are small and of the same sign for all modes, so they cannot yet be distinguished from an instrumental offset, while ROA was negligibly small at 633 nm.

issues.claim: Calculations show ROA originates from ferroaxial order
issues.headline: Tight-binding model is not connected to NiTiO3 yet claims too much
issues.issue: The model uses spinless p orbitals with hand-chosen hoppings, arbitrary ω units and a single phenomenological phonon vertex, while the experimental resonance is a localized Ni2+ d-d multiplet excitation, and no mapping to 785/633/532 nm is given. The sign of I_LR - I_RL changes several times with ω in Fig. 4, so the model predicts neither sign nor magnitude at the experimental energy and shows only what symmetry already implies.

evidence.quote: Furthermore, our calculations show that the observed NROA originates directly from the ferroaxial order.

issues.fix: Reword the 'reveal'/'show that the observed NROA originates directly from the ferroaxial order' and 'support the experimental results obtained with different light sources' statements as a symmetry-level, minimal-model proof of principle. Alternatively tie the model to NiTiO3 (d orbitals, realistic crystal field, ω mapped to measured transitions, mode-resolved vertex), justify the parameters and show linear scaling with t_ax at small t_ax.

issues.headline: Mode dependence of g_ROA, including opposite signs, is unexplained
issues.issue: Table S4 shows E_g(1) and E_g(2) with opposite signs on the same face, E_g(4) near zero and unequal front/back magnitudes for E_g(2) and E_g(3), but the only explanation is an unquantified statement that E_g(1) has the largest Ni displacement. Nothing explains the sign of E_g(2) or why E_g(4) vanishes, and the single-vertex model cannot distinguish modes.

evidence.quote: leading to the strongest coupling to the resonant transition and accounting for the largest observed ROA at 785 nm

issues.fix: Tabulate the Ni (and Ti, O) displacement amplitudes or projected Ni weight of each E_g eigenvector from the DFT calculation next to g_ROA and plot |g_ROA| against them, ideally compute complex Raman tensors per mode; otherwise state explicitly that mode-dependent signs and magnitudes are not addressed.
issues.fix_scoped: These results suggest that NROA is selectively enhanced in certain phonon modes, although the mode-dependent signs and magnitudes of gROA are not explained by the present analysis.

edit_scoped.before: These results suggest that NROA is selectively enhanced in certain phonon modes due to coupling with the electronic structure associated with the ferroaxial order.
edit_scoped.after: These results suggest that NROA is selectively enhanced in certain phonon modes, although the mode-dependent signs and magnitudes of gROA are not explained by the present analysis.

issues.issue: All quantitative data come from one 60 µm single-domain crystal, and the multidomain crystal was made by annealing the same crystal above T_C. Reproducibility on a second crystal or face preparation is not shown, and whether the faces were polished is not stated.

evidence.quote: A multidomain crystal was obtained by heating a single-domain crystal to 1620 K and then slowly cooling it, resulting in a mixture of ferroaxial domains.

issues.headline: Acquisition parameters missing and resonant laser heating not checked
issues.issue: Laser power at the sample, objective NA, spot size for Fig. 3, integration times and confocal depth of focus are not reported. At 785 nm the excitation is resonantly absorbed so local heating is possible, and a high-NA objective depolarizes circular light.

evidence.quote: The scattered light was collected through an objective lens, filtered to remove Rayleigh scattering using edge/notch filters, and detected with a CCD-equipped spectrometer.

issues.fix: Report these parameters, estimate the local temperature from the anti-Stokes/Stokes ratio of E_g(1) in Fig. 3, and show that g_ROA does not depend on laser power.
issues.fix_scoped: All measurements were performed at a nominal temperature of 295 K (local laser heating was not assessed), which is far above the antiferromagnetic Néel temperature, TN = 22.5 K [26].

issues.claim: Resonance couples selectively to ferroaxial order
issues.headline: Claimed lowering of Ni site symmetry from 3m to 3 is incorrect
issues.issue: In corundum R-3c the cation site already has site symmetry 3, as does the Ni site in R-3; the ordering removes the c-glide, not point symmetry at the cation site, and Sec. S3 itself gives the Ni site symmetry as 3. This statement motivates why the d-d resonance couples to the ferroaxial order.

evidence.quote: The ferroaxial rotational distortion further lowers the local symmetry from 3m to 3, which modifies the symmetry of the lattice displacements coupled to the d-d transition.

issues.fix: Correct the statement and reformulate the argument in terms of the loss of the c-glide and the resulting d ≠ 0 tensor component.

issues.headline: Stokes/anti-Stokes non-magnetic argument is asserted, not derived
issues.issue: The rule is transferred from molecular ROA without showing it applies to the degenerate 1E_g/2E_g pair in this geometry, and the model check is uninformative because δω = ±10^-3 is far below the smearing η = 0.01. At 295 K, well above T_N with no net magnetization, a magnetic origin is already unlikely, so the test adds little.

evidence.quote: is non-magnetic in origin, in contrast to magnetic ROA where the sign reverses

issues.fix: Either derive the time-reversal/Stokes-anti-Stokes relation for cross-circular backscattering from a T-even axial order in -3 under resonance and evaluate the model at realistic δω, or present the test as a consistency check only.

issues.headline: Comparison with molecular ROA and 'natural ROA' label are misleading
issues.issue: Molecular natural ROA (g ~ 10^-3) is a reciprocal, orientationally averaged dipole-interference effect in transparent media, whereas here the signal is a directional, resonance-enabled electric-dipole effect following A·k that averages to zero over orientations. Comparing the two magnitudes compares different physics.

evidence.quote: This value is several orders of magnitude larger than the typical NROA of chiral molecules

issues.fix: Remove or qualify the 10^-3 comparison, give the cross-circular asymmetries reported for 1T-TaS2 and NiCo2TeO6 as the benchmark, and clarify that the observable is a directional cross-circular intensity difference governed by A·k, possibly with a clearer name.

issues.issue: In Eqs. S32-S33 the step from time reversal plus reality to Q1 = Q2 is unclear, since time reversal normally maps 1E_g onto 2E_g with complex conjugation; |Q1| = |Q2| follows simply from the degeneracy. The parameter α2 in Eqs. S64-S65 is not defined.

issues.fix: State that |Q1| = |Q2| follows from the 1E_g/2E_g degeneracy enforced by time reversal, and define α2.
